text:
The <u>Southern sea otter</u> and <u>ribbon seal</u> are clearly associated with the marine biome. Considerably reduced by severe slaughter during late 1800's, the southern sea otter now has a potential for reoccupying much of its former range along the West Coast from Washington to central Baja, California. The ribbon seal, however, apparently has always existed in small numbers in its natural range in the Bering Sea.
Although the whooping crane is rather restricted in its range at the present time, nesting in Wood Buffalo National Park well within the coniferous forest biome in Canada and wintering in the vicinity of Aransas National Wildlife Refuge on the Texas Gulf Coast, it once ranged in the course of its annual cycle over a wide expanse of the grassland biome. It is likely that restoration efforts will succeed in establishing one or two additional flocks related even more closely to the grassland biome.
Fifteen additional species and subspecies now listed in the U.S. "Red Book" have widespread ranges more or less related to biomes, but these animals have special requirements which are limiting within the biome (Appendix E).

Most require an aquatic or moist environment. For example, a supply of prey fish free from contamination by pesticides is required for a healthy population of Southern bald eagles. With curtailment of contaminated food chains and successful protection or restoration of nest sites, we should be able to return this symbol of our nation to many estuarine areas and large freshwater bodies in the southern half of the contiguous United States.
The American alligator is associated with swampy marshy areas in low areas of the southern temperate deciduous hardwood biome. The species once ranged from North Carolina on the Atlantic Coastal Plain to Florida and westward along the Gulf Coast to the Rio Grande and including the Mississippi
